title: Python leads technology mentions in Hacker News hiring posts
text: The fact that I studied R led me to question how classroom programming stacks up against the technologies referred to in job advertisements. For a person looking into technology careers, would learning Python, web development, or cloud infrastructure be a useful next move? I collected two of the Hacker News “Who is hiring?” threads and then compared them using a fixed list of 20 technology categories. Python is mentioned in 27.7% of the hiring comments that remained from September 2026, which is the highest proportion among the categories in question, while I was surprised to find out that R appears in 0 of 256 postings. Python is a reasonable place to start for this kind of job. However, the analysis does not indicate which skill will yield the highest payoff or increase an individual’s chances of getting an offer.

title: Python leads technology mentions in Hacker News hiring posts
text:
Where the data comes from
The data comes from the September 2025 and September 2026 threads. The acquisition metadata were saved on 19 September 2026. I used an R scraper with rvest to collect public HTML, cache the pages, and wait 30 seconds between each new page request. The current robots.txt asks for this delay and allows access to /item. The workflow does not get around logins, paywalls, or CAPTCHAs. While Hacker News has an official API, I used HTML extraction to practice the rvest workflow required for this assignment. No new requests are needed to reproduce the saved analysis.

title: Python leads technology mentions in Hacker News hiring posts
text:
Turning comments into measurements
The files contain 863 comments, some of which are replies. I kept the top-level comments that include text, removed duplicate comment IDs, and excluded 10 entries identified during review as discussions, personal job-seeking or service offers, or insufficiently informative content. The final dataset consists of 294 hiring comments from 2025 and 256 from 2026. The IDs of the excluded entries together with the reasons for their exclusion are saved with the code. Each comment is counted only once even if it promotes more than one job; likewise, the same employer can be listed more than once.
Keyword matching also has to be checked. I only caught the “Go” bug because its count jumped from 26 to 42 between two runs on identical data, triggered by phrases like “Go for it” and “Go-To-Market”. Updating the matching rules resolved those false positives and captured the all-caps GO spelling. For the other options, the criteria are intentionally kept narrow: SQL counts the single term, while Postgres includes PostgreSQL. It is not appropriate to add the percentages since comments can refer to both. These adjustments cover mentions such as company technology stacks, not the verified requirements for each advertised role.


Show code
knitr::include_graphics(file.path(POST_DIR, "results", "figures", "skill_share_2026.png"))








Figure 1: Leading technology categories in retained September 2026 hiring comments. Ties at rank 12 are included.

title: Python leads technology mentions in Hacker News hiring posts
section: What was the difference between the two snapshots?
text:
What was the difference between the two snapshots?
TypeScript and React make up 20.3% and 19.9% of the retained comments from 2026, respectively. Their proportions are 8.3 and 8.0 percentage points lower than in the 2025 snapshot. These are the observed differences, not an indication of a widespread decline in demand for web development.
Comparing two September threads eliminates one aspect of the seasonal mismatch by using the same calendar month, but it does not keep the hiring population constant. The September 2026 data was still incomplete at the time of collection, and each thread includes different employers and positions. Because this is a self-selecting online community, not a random selection of jobs, keyword rules may also miss abbreviations or count occasional references. For these reasons I give the comparison only a descriptive account rather than treating these differences as evidence about the wider labour market.


Show code
knitr::include_graphics(file.path(POST_DIR, "results", "figures", "skill_change.png"))








Figure 2: Observed differences in mention shares across the two saved September threads. These are descriptive comparisons, not causal effects or population estimates.

title: Python leads technology mentions in Hacker News hiring posts
section: What is the right thing for a student to do in this situation?
text:
What is the right thing for a student to do in this situation?
If a student is already using R and wants to learn about the types of jobs listed here, I suggest they create a small Python project by obtaining data, cleaning it, and publishing a reproducible analysis. While Python is prominent, such a project should be seen as a reasonable experiment rather than a sure way to secure a job. Alternatively, a student aiming for a career in web development could build a TypeScript/React application, since both are still frequently mentioned even though they have lower proportions in this comparison.
Before you decide on a longer course, look at a selection of advertisements that correspond to your location, level of experience, and the position you want. Determine which technologies are essential and which only refer to the employer’s technology stack. This matters because the dataset includes senior engineering positions, junior ones, and non-technical roles. The lack of a verified R keyword match in this case does not prove that R is unimportant for jobs in economics or statistics.


Show code
trend |>
  transmute(Category = skill,
            `2025 count` = n_2025,
            `2025 (%)` = round(100 * share_2025, 1),
            `2026 count` = n_2026,
            `2026 (%)` = round(100 * share_2026, 1),
            `Change (pp)` = round(change_pp, 1)) |>
  knitr::kable()

title: A college county and the Poconos stand out for rent pressure
text:
Rent competes with groceries, the trip to work, and the money set aside for an emergency. When it takes a larger share of a household’s income, something else has to give. An apartment can look inexpensive compared with Philadelphia and still be difficult to afford on a local paycheck.
That is why the geography matters. If housing assistance is planned around the assumption that rent pressure belongs mainly to the biggest city, renters elsewhere can be overlooked. Centre County, home to State College, and Monroe County in the Poconos challenge that picture. Both stand out on the map below.
I count households spending at least 30% of their income on rent and utilities. Crossing that line does not suddenly make a household unable to cope, but it flags how much of the budget housing absorbs. In Census estimates covering 2020 through 2024, 52.3% of Philadelphia renters met that threshold, compared with 47.2% across the rest of Pennsylvania. The share was higher in the city, yet nearly half of renters elsewhere also met the threshold.
Here, “renters” means households paying rent whose rent share of income can be calculated. The comparison excludes households paying no rent or reporting zero or negative income. These are survey estimates spanning five years, not a snapshot of today’s rental market.
The map covers all 67 counties. Darker colors show a larger share of renters meeting the threshold. They do not show higher rents or more households.








Figure 1: Centre and several eastern counties stand out; estimates for small counties such as Forest, Cameron, and Elk are less precise than the colors suggest.





Centre’s share was 57.0%, almost identical to Monroe’s 57.0%. Lehigh and Delaware also had high shares. These places do not all have the same housing market, which is part of the point.
Centre’s 2023 housing assessment connects high burdens in student neighborhoods near Penn State partly to low student incomes. The mix of renters may therefore help explain its position, without telling us that students face no hardship. Monroe’s housing study describes people relocating from costlier New York and New Jersey alongside a shortage of rentals affordable at local incomes. In the Lehigh Valley, planners identify housing construction that has lagged population growth. These reports suggest possible explanations; the map cannot measure their contribution.
Nor can color settle a ranking. The next chart shows the six highest county estimates, plus Allegheny as a western urban comparison. The error bars show how precise each number is. Centre and Monroe should not be treated as a clear first and second place.








Figure 2: Philadelphia has a lower share than Centre but far more households meeting the threshold.





The counts change the story. Philadelphia had about 159,500 households meeting the threshold, compared with 11,800 in Centre. Philadelphia alone accounted for 22.1% of the statewide total. Allegheny’s lower share still represented about 82,100 households. A darker county is not automatically where assistance could reach the most renters. Shares show how widespread the pressure is locally; counts show how many households are affected.
The pressure is often more than a narrow crossing of the 30% line. Statewide, 24.9% of renters spent at least half their income on housing. That leaves at most half for everything else. For a housing organization, the lesson is to look beyond Philadelphia without losing sight of the much larger number of households affected there.
County averages cannot identify which families need help or separate the effects of low incomes and high rents. Excluded households can also face hardship. The map is a starting point for deciding where to look more closely, not a substitute for understanding local households.
The main takeaways are:

Rent pressure reaches college communities and the Poconos as well as Philadelphia.
Philadelphia’s share is higher than the rest of the state’s, but nearly half of renters elsewhere also meet the threshold.
Centre’s high share and Philadelphia’s much larger count point to different scales of housing need. Assistance planning should consider both.

Data come from the Census Bureau’s 2020 to 2024 ACS table B25070, its variance replicate estimates, and 2024 county boundaries. GitHub repository.

title: Inflation fell first, unemployment rose later: The U.S. experience through 2024
text:
In 2022, bringing inflation down raised an uncomfortable question. Would relief at the checkout come at the cost of more people losing work? Some prominent economists warned of a substantial rise in unemployment, while others thought inflation could ease without a painful recession. For households already struggling with rising bills, the possibility of losing a paycheck made the stakes especially high.
Did unemployment rise throughout the fall in inflation, or mainly later? I focus on mid-2022 through 2024, the two and a half years after the inflation peak.
One reason to expect a tradeoff is that strong spending can encourage hiring while also pushing prices up. Slowing spending could ease price pressure but weaken hiring. This is one idea behind the Phillips curve.
Inflation measures how much prices increased compared with the same month a year earlier. The unemployment rate counts people without a job who are available and actively looking for work, as a percentage of everyone working or looking for work. Falling inflation means prices rise more slowly, not that prices fall.
The first chart shows why timing matters. Inflation peaked at 9.0% in June 2022 and fell sharply afterward. By December 2024, unemployment had risen 0.5 percentage points from peak inflation, or 0.7 points from its later low.








Figure 1: Inflation began falling before unemployment began its sustained rise.





In July 2024, unemployment had risen enough to trigger the Sahm rule, a widely watched recession warning. Yet no recession followed through the end of 2024. The warning called for caution, but did not mean the soft landing had failed.
Was this simply a predictable exchange between inflation and jobs? The second chart checks whether similar unemployment consistently came with similar inflation. Each point represents one month, grouped into 2015 through 2019 before COVID, the disruption in 2020 and 2021, and the inflation and cooling period from 2022 through 2024.








Figure 2: Months with similar unemployment had very different inflation rates across the three periods.





Unemployment was 3.6% in December 2019 and 3.6% in June 2022. Yet inflation was 2.3% in the first month and 9.0% in the second. Similar unemployment accompanied very different inflation. Unemployment alone does not explain the price pressures households faced.
How could inflation fall without a collapse in hiring? In his August 2024 Jackson Hole speech, Federal Reserve Chair Jerome Powell described strong spending colliding with disrupted supply chains, followed by energy price shocks after Russia invaded Ukraine. He argued that easing those disruptions helped bring inflation down alongside slower demand. The headline consumer price index includes energy, so those price swings also affect the inflation measure used here.
The final chart shows how that adjustment unfolded over time. Each point averages three months to make the path easier to follow. Moving downward means inflation fell; moving right means unemployment rose. The chart zooms in on the smaller unemployment changes.








Figure 3: The arrows trace an early fall in inflation followed by a clearer rise in unemployment.





Much of the initial movement was downward. From 2022 Q2 to 2023 Q2, inflation fell from 8.6% to 4.1%, while unemployment stayed close to 3.5%.
Afterward, the path moved more clearly to the right. By 2024 Q4, unemployment averaged 4.1% and inflation 2.7%.
Through the end of 2024, this pattern was closer to the soft landing view than to predictions that bringing inflation down would require a large, sustained rise in joblessness. Most of the inflation decline arrived before the clearer unemployment increase. The later warning signal qualifies that favorable outcome rather than erasing it.
These charts cannot establish which policies or supply changes caused the outcome, and small movements in survey estimates should not be treated as exact population changes. The conclusion applies to this period and these national averages, not to every household or what happened after 2024.
The main takeaways are:

Much of the fall in inflation came before the clearer rise in unemployment.
The experience through 2024 was closer to a soft landing, but the later unemployment rise was a meaningful warning.
Similar unemployment came with very different inflation, so unemployment alone does not explain price pressure.

Data come from BLS via FRED’s consumer price index and unemployment rate. The GitHub repository contains the data, code, methods, and instructions for reproducing the analysis.

title: Did labor-force participation recover equally across age groups?
text:
A low unemployment rate does not tell us whether people are participating in the labor market. Someone who stops looking for work generally leaves the unemployment-rate denominator. Labor-force participation asks a different question: what share of the population is working or looking for work? That distinction matters when comparing younger adults, people in their main working years, and older adults.
I analyze IPUMS CPS microdata in order to determine participation levels in 2024 relative to the levels in 2019. The overall annual participation rate decreased from 63.4% to 62.9%, which means that participation in 2024 was 0.5 percentage points lower than in 2019. The figures below present how that aggregate comparison relates to participation within age groups and changes in the population’s age mix.

title: Did labor-force participation recover equally across age groups?
text:
A low unemployment rate does not tell us whether people are participating in the labor market. Someone who stops looking for work generally leaves the unemployment-rate denominator. Labor-force participation asks a different question: what share of the population is working or looking for work? That distinction matters when comparing younger adults, people in their main working years, and older adults.
I analyze IPUMS CPS microdata in order to determine participation levels in 2024 relative to the levels in 2019. The overall annual participation rate decreased from 63.4% to 62.9%, which means that participation in 2024 was 0.5 percentage points lower than in 2019. The figures below present how that aggregate comparison relates to participation within age groups and changes in the population’s age mix.

title: Did labor-force participation recover equally across age groups?
text:
Measuring participation consistently
The analysis covers civilians aged 16 and older across all 72 Basic Monthly CPS samples from January 2019 through December 2024. Each month’s rate is the share working or looking for work, using WTFINL sampling weights to represent the population. Annual estimates average the twelve monthly rates equally. The repository explains the sample selection and weighting in detail.

title: Did labor-force participation recover equally across age groups?
text:
First, compare recovery paths








Figure 1: Annual means of monthly weighted participation rates, expressed as changes from 2019. Panels use identical percentage-point scales; zero marks each group’s baseline.





Figure 1 shows changes from 2019 across four stages of working life. By 2024, participation among adults aged 25 to 54 was 1.0 percentage points above its baseline. Adults aged 55 to 64 gained 0.7 points, while those aged 16 to 24 were approximately unchanged, gaining 0.1 points. Adults aged 65 and older were the only group still below baseline, down 0.8 points.
All four groups declined between 2019 and 2020. Adults aged 16 to 24 had the deepest drop, 2.4 percentage points, possibly reflecting disruption to entry-level work. Their participation rebounded above baseline in 2023 before falling back toward it in 2024. The contrasting outcomes for adults aged 55 to 64 and those aged 65 and older show why treating all older adults as one group would hide part of the recovery.

title: Did labor-force participation recover equally across age groups?
section: Next, look at who makes up the population
text:
Next, look at who makes up the population








Figure 2: Changes in each age group’s share of the civilian population aged 16 and older, using annual averages of monthly weighted shares.





Figure 2 introduces the other part of the story. Adults aged 65 and older grew from 20.4% to 22.2% of the population in this analysis. The shares of the three younger groups fell. This matters because participation in 2024 was 19.9% among adults aged 65 and older, compared with 83.7% among those aged 25 to 54. A growing share of people in a group with lower participation can pull down the overall rate even when participation improves within most groups.

title: Did labor-force participation recover equally across age groups?
section: Finally, hold the age mix fixed
text:
Finally, hold the age mix fixed
To separate these two influences, I calculate each month’s overall rate twice. Let \(s_{g,y,m}\) be age group \(g\)’s population share and \(p_{g,y,m}\) its participation rate in year \(y\), month \(m\).
\[
P_{y,m}=\sum_g s_{g,y,m}p_{g,y,m}
\qquad\text{(observed)}
\]
\[
P^{\mathrm{fixed}}_{y,m}=\sum_g s_{g,2019,m}p_{g,y,m}
\qquad\text{(2019 age mix)}
\]
The second calculation keeps the same participation rates but substitutes the corresponding month’s 2019 population shares. For example, January 2024 uses January 2019 shares. I then average each set of twelve monthly rates. Only the shares differ, so the gap isolates the composition effect under this calculation.








Figure 3: Overall participation changes, observed and standardized to 2019 age-group shares. Both series equal zero in 2019 by construction.





Figure 3 expresses both series as changes from their common 2019 baseline. With the age mix held fixed, participation in 2024 was 0.4 percentage points higher than in 2019. The observed shortfall becomes a modest increase.
In levels, observed participation in 2024 was 62.86%, compared with 63.85% using the 2019 age mix. The gap was 0.99 percentage points. That difference describes the contribution of changing age shares under this standardization; it does not estimate what a policy would accomplish.

title: Did labor-force participation recover equally across age groups?
text:
Takeaway and limits
The CPS has a complex rotating design, and pandemic-era collection disruptions complicate interpretation. These comparisons do not establish causes or statistical significance. Annual averages hide monthly changes, and broad age groups hide differences within them. This analysis does not follow a fixed cohort.

Participation recovered differently across age groups, with adults aged 65 and older still below their 2019 rate.
The population also shifted toward that older group, which has much lower participation.
Holding the age mix fixed turns the overall shortfall into a modest increase. The aggregate rate alone misses this distinction.


Data: Flood et al. (2025), IPUMS CPS: Version 13.0, University of Minnesota. Basic Monthly samples, January 2019 through December 2024; extract created September 27, 2026. The analysis uses 6,146,546 eligible person-month observations, not unique individuals.
Code and replication: Blog repository. The post folder contains the R analysis, aggregate results, figures, and replication instructions. Raw microdata are excluded from Git.

title: What a p-value actually tells you
text:
Imagine reading a report about a training course that gives \(p=0.03\) for an increase in participants’ test scores. Does that mean its conclusion has a 97% probability of being correct? No. The difference matters to anyone who must act on the result, such as a company deciding whether to pay for the course for all of its staff. The question this post answers is: what probability does a p-value actually measure, and what can we conclude from it? Rather than stopping at the textbook definition, I build a world in which the course does nothing and count how often that world still produces a result this large.
This distinction is important enough that the American Statistical Association’s statement on p-values explicitly addresses it. A p-value does not give the probability that the tested hypothesis is true. To see what it does give, we need to separate two questions that sound similar.

title: What a p-value actually tells you
text:
Imagine reading a report about a training course that gives \(p=0.03\) for an increase in participants’ test scores. Does that mean its conclusion has a 97% probability of being correct? No. The difference matters to anyone who must act on the result, such as a company deciding whether to pay for the course for all of its staff. The question this post answers is: what probability does a p-value actually measure, and what can we conclude from it? Rather than stopping at the textbook definition, I build a world in which the course does nothing and count how often that world still produces a result this large.
This distinction is important enough that the American Statistical Association’s statement on p-values explicitly addresses it. A p-value does not give the probability that the tested hypothesis is true. To see what it does give, we need to separate two questions that sound similar.

title: What a p-value actually tells you
section: Start with the direction of the question
text:
Start with the direction of the question
We often want to ask, “Given these results, how plausible is my hypothesis?” A significance test instead asks, “If the null model were correct, how often would results this extreme or more extreme occur?” The first question concerns the hypothesis after seeing the data; the second concerns possible data under an assumed hypothesis.
An analogy helps: knowing that a professional basketball player is likely to be tall does not tell us that a tall person is likely to be a professional basketball player. Reversing the condition changes the question. In statistics, a posterior probability such as \(P(H_0\mid\text{data})\) requires a model for the alternatives and prior probabilities, not just a p-value.
To see the difference in numbers, the next section builds the world described at the start: one where the course does nothing on average.

title: What a p-value actually tells you
text:
Build a simple null world
Suppose 30 trainees take a test before and after a course, with an average score increase of 0.34 standardized units. We test whether the population’s mean score change is positive. Assume these changes are independent and normally distributed with a known standard deviation of 1. These are teaching assumptions, not data from an actual study. A score increase alone would not establish that the course caused it.
The null hypothesis is \(H_0:\mu=0\), and the alternative is \(H_1:\mu>0\). Because we specify a positive direction in advance, this is a one-sided test. Its p-value is
\[
p=P(\bar X\geq 0.34\mid\mu=0,\text{ assumed sampling model}).
\]
Here, \(\bar X\) is the sample mean. Under the null, it varies around zero with standard deviation \(1/\sqrt{30}\). The p-value measures the right-tail probability beyond 0.34. It does not measure the probability of observing exactly 0.34 or the probability that \(\mu=0\).

title: What a p-value actually tells you
section: Use simulation to make the probability visible
text:
Use simulation to make the probability visible
The R code below repeats this hypothetical experiment 10,000 times. Each repetition draws 30 observations from the null model and records their mean. Counting the means at least as large as 0.34 approximates the probability in the equation. Simulation is useful here because it turns an abstract conditional probability into a fraction of repeated experiments.

set.seed(42)                 # Make the simulation reproducible.
n <- 30
obs_stat <- 0.34
repetitions <- 10000
null_stats <- replicate(repetitions, mean(rnorm(n, mean = 0, sd = 1)))
p_sim <- mean(null_stats >= obs_stat)
p_exact <- pnorm(obs_stat, mean = 0, sd = 1 / sqrt(n), lower.tail = FALSE)
stopifnot(abs(p_sim - p_exact) < 5 * sqrt(p_exact * (1 - p_exact) / repetitions))

rnorm() generates observations, replicate() repeats the experiment, and the final mean() of the comparison counts the fraction meeting our threshold. pnorm() calculates the exact normal tail probability for comparison; it does not simulate another set of experiments.
The final stopifnot() checks that the simulated probability is close to the exact answer, allowing a margin of five simulation standard errors for random variation. This is a sanity check on the simulation, not the hypothesis test.








Figure 1: Simulated average score changes under the null (histogram), with their exact normal density (blue). The orange area under the curve is the exact one-sided p-value beyond the observed mean of 0.34.





The simulated fraction is 2.9%, close to the exact value of 3.13%. We built a world with no average score change, yet about 3 in every 100 repetitions still crossed the observed line. The small difference between simulation and calculation is Monte Carlo variation. A two-sided test would also count equally extreme negative means and answer a different question.

title: What a p-value actually tells you
text:
What should we conclude?
The observed mean is unusual under the specified null model, providing evidence against it. But every simulated experiment assumed the null was true: we never generated a mixture of true and false hypotheses. The simulation therefore cannot tell us what fraction of hypotheses are true after a small p-value appears.
Nor does a small p-value establish that an effect is economically important. Here, the estimated mean is 0.34 standardized units; its practical meaning depends on the outcome and context. For the company, \(p=0.03\) is a reason to take the score gain seriously, not proof that the course works. It would still need to weigh the size of the gain against the course’s cost, and without a comparison group it cannot tell whether the course caused the gain. Assumptions, uncertainty, study design, and whether the test was chosen before looking at the data also matter. A large p-value, conversely, would not prove that the mean is zero.
The main takeaways are:

A p-value describes how unusual the observed result is under a specified model.
A value of \(p=0.03\) does not mean the conclusion is “97% certain.” That is a question the test never calculated.
Report the size and uncertainty of the score change, and consider the study design before deciding what it means.

title: What a p-value actually tells you
text:
Reference
Wasserstein, R. L., and Lazar, N. A. (2016). The ASA’s Statement on p-Values: Context, Process, and Purpose. The American Statistician, 70(2), pages 129 to 133.

title: How one year of income can mislead a study of mobility
text:
Could income mobility look stronger simply because we measured people in the wrong year? A parent might receive an unusually large bonus, while their adult child is still building a career. Neither income necessarily reflects what that person usually earns. Mistaking these temporary differences for lasting ones could make economic opportunity appear more open than it is.
This has happened in real research. Solon (1992) showed that earlier U.S. estimates were biased downward by measurement error, unrepresentative samples, or both; using the Panel Study of Income Dynamics, he found a long-run intergenerational correlation of at least 0.4, implying much less mobility than earlier work suggested. Mazumder (2005) later used Social Security earnings histories and found that averaging fathers’ earnings over only a few years understated the elasticity by roughly 30% or more, putting it near 0.6. How income was measured changed what economists concluded about opportunity in the United States.
To see why, I use SQL inside Python to match 7,166 children from 4,000 simulated families to their parents. The database copies the structure of the Panel Study of Income Dynamics (PSID), but every value is simulated; no PSID data are used. Averaging several years reveals a stronger income connection than a single year does, even though the families are unchanged. These are teaching data with a known underlying relationship, not estimates for the United States.

title: How one year of income can mislead a study of mobility
section: Match the people before comparing their incomes
text:
Match the people before comparing their incomes
Follow the README’s setup instructions, then run python run.py and python tutorial.py from this post’s folder. The first builds the data and SQLite database; the second runs the matching and comparisons below. Four tables carry the analysis, each modeled on a PSID file described in its public documentation.








Table
One row represents
Important columns




individuals
A person
id68, pn, birth_year, sex


parent_links
A child and one parent
child and parent id68 and pn, parent_type


individual_years
A person in a survey year
id68, pn, year, interview_number, sequence_number


family_years
A family in a survey year
year, interview_number, family_income



Three features of the real survey shape the query. First, no single column identifies a person: the 1968 family ID (id68) and the person number (pn) do so together, so every join uses both. Second, parent_links has one row per parent, like the PSID’s parent map, so a child with a mother and a father appears twice. Third, income belongs to families, not people. A family’s interview number is valid for one survey year only, so a person’s income comes from finding that year’s interview number in individual_years and then the matching row in family_years. Following the PSID’s guidance, I keep years in which the person was the reference person or spouse (sequence number 1 or 2). In the real PSID, the parent map comes from its FIMS tool, and a study must still decide how to treat parents who live apart, siblings, and people who leave the survey.
Parents and children reach the same age in different calendar years, so I measure parental income by the child’s age: the years when the child was 15 to 19. The query in sql/match.sql also summarizes each person’s income before joining the generations; joining two five-year histories first would produce 25 combinations per pair.
WITH parent_family_years AS (
    -- One row per child and year: the income of the family in which the
    -- child's parent was reference person or spouse. DISTINCT keeps one row
    -- when the mother and father lived in the same family that year.
    SELECT DISTINCT l.child_id68, l.child_pn, y.year, y.interview_number,
           f.family_income
    FROM parent_links AS l
    JOIN individuals AS c
      ON c.id68 = l.child_id68 AND c.pn = l.child_pn
    JOIN individual_years AS y
      ON y.id68 = l.parent_id68 AND y.pn = l.parent_pn
    JOIN family_years AS f
      ON f.year = y.year AND f.interview_number = y.interview_number
    WHERE y.sequence_number IN (1, 2)
      AND y.relation_to_rp IN ('reference person', 'spouse')
      AND y.year - c.birth_year BETWEEN :p_start AND :p_end
),
parent_income AS (
    SELECT child_id68, child_pn, AVG(family_income) AS parent_income
    FROM parent_family_years
    GROUP BY child_id68, child_pn
    HAVING COUNT(*) = :p_years
       AND COUNT(DISTINCT year) = :p_years
),
child_income AS (
    SELECT c.id68, c.pn, AVG(f.family_income) AS child_income
    FROM individuals AS c
    JOIN individual_years AS y
      ON y.id68 = c.id68 AND y.pn = c.pn
    JOIN family_years AS f
      ON f.year = y.year AND f.interview_number = y.interview_number
    WHERE y.sequence_number IN (1, 2)
      AND y.relation_to_rp IN ('reference person', 'spouse')
      AND y.year - c.birth_year BETWEEN :c_start AND :c_end
    GROUP BY c.id68, c.pn
    HAVING COUNT(*) = :c_years
       AND COUNT(DISTINCT y.year) = :c_years
)
SELECT p.child_id68 AS id68, p.child_pn AS pn,
       p.parent_income, c.child_income
FROM parent_income AS p
JOIN child_income AS c
  ON c.id68 = p.child_id68 AND c.pn = p.child_pn
ORDER BY id68, pn;
The query works in four steps.

Find each parent’s family in each year. The first WITH block starts from parent_links and uses JOIN to attach the parent’s rows in individual_years, matching both parts of the ID. A second join attaches that year’s family income from family_years, matching year and interview_number. SELECT keeps only what later steps need.
Line the generations up by the child’s age. y.year - c.birth_year turns each survey year into the child’s age, and WHERE ... BETWEEN :p_start AND :p_end keeps only the chosen ages. Names that begin with a colon are placeholders that Python fills in, so one query serves every comparison below.
Remove the duplicate from two parents, then average. When a mother and father live in the same family, both of their rows find the same family-year, so SELECT DISTINCT keeps one copy. GROUP BY then gathers each child’s years, the aggregate function AVG(family_income) turns them into one number, and HAVING requires exactly one family for every requested year. Without DISTINCT, the average would hide the problem, but each two-parent child would have ten rows instead of five, and the completeness check would silently drop 6,095 of the 7,166 children.
Repeat for the child, then join. The child_income block applies the same logic to the child’s own family in adulthood. The final SELECT joins the two summaries on the child’s id68 and pn, producing one row per child with both generations’ incomes.

With parental income over the child’s ages 15 to 19 and the child’s income over ages 40 to 44, the first rows of the result look like this. Each income is a five-year average of family income in constant dollars. The first two children were born in the same year, so they share a parental average; their sister was born five years later, so her parents’ income is measured over different years.

The Python helper sends the age limits to this query and retrieves a pandas table. Changing those limits lets us compare income measures without changing the families.


Show the Python helper that runs the SQL query

from pathlib import Path
import sqlite3
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd

POST = Path(__file__).resolve().parent
query = (POST / "sql/match.sql").read_text()

def match(conn, parent_window, child_ages):
    """Match children to parental and own family income.

    parent_window: the child's ages when parental income is measured.
    child_ages: the child's ages when the child's own income is measured.
    """
    p0, p1 = parent_window
    c0, c1 = child_ages
    params = dict(p_start=p0, p_end=p1, p_years=p1 - p0 + 1,
                  c_start=c0, c_end=c1, c_years=c1 - c0 + 1)
    return pd.read_sql_query(query, conn, params=params)

title: How one year of income can mislead a study of mobility
section: Estimate persistence, then change the measurement window
text:
Estimate persistence, then change the measurement window
How closely do the generations’ incomes move together? The intergenerational elasticity, or IGE, measures that connection. With the model’s IGE of 0.40, 10% higher parental income is associated with about 4% higher child income. A smaller value suggests less persistence and more mobility. It is an association, not a causal effect.
To estimate it, fit a line to the natural logarithms of the matched incomes. The slope, \(\beta\), is the IGE.
\[
\log(\text{child income}) = \alpha + \beta\log(\text{parent income}) + \varepsilon.
\]
SQL averages annual income amounts in constant dollars before Python takes logarithms. In the code, np.ones supplies the intercept and np.linalg.lstsq fits the line. The checks keep each child once and the children identical across comparisons.


Show the Python code that estimates and compares the slopes

def ige(pairs):
    x = np.log(pairs["parent_income"].to_numpy())
    y = np.log(pairs["child_income"].to_numpy())
    X = np.column_stack([np.ones(len(x)), x])
    intercept, slope = np.linalg.lstsq(X, y, rcond=None)[0]
    return float(slope)

def compare(conn):
    single = match(conn, (15, 15), (40, 40))
    averaged = match(conn, (15, 19), (40, 44))
    young = match(conn, (15, 19), (25, 29))
    for pairs in (single, averaged, young):
        assert not pairs.duplicated(["id68", "pn"]).any()
        assert pairs[["id68", "pn"]].equals(single[["id68", "pn"]])
        assert (pairs[["parent_income", "child_income"]] > 0).all().all()
    return pd.DataFrame({
        "measure": ["One year for each generation",
                    "Five-year averages for each generation",
                    "Five-year averages, child aged 25 to 29"],
        "pairs": [len(single), len(averaged), len(young)],
        "ige": [ige(single), ige(averaged), ige(young)]
    })

if __name__ == "__main__":
    with sqlite3.connect(POST / "data/mobility.sqlite") as conn:
        print(compare(conn).to_string(index=False, float_format="%.3f"))

Using one year for each generation, the parents’ family income when the child was 15 and the child’s at 40, gives 0.20. Averaging five years for each raises it to 0.30, closer to the model’s 0.40. The families did not become less mobile. Better measurement revealed more of the income connection already built into the simulation.








Figure 1: Averaging several years reduces the distortion from temporary income fluctuations in this simulation.





Temporary swings in parental income blur its relationship with the child’s income, pushing the slope toward zero. Averaging reduces that distortion. Independent swings in child income mainly make estimates less precise. Five years still imperfectly measure lasting income, and chance also affects this simulated sample.

title: How one year of income can mislead a study of mobility
section: Averaging cannot fix measuring children too young
text:
Averaging cannot fix measuring children too young
But does averaging solve the whole problem? Holding parental income at its five-year average, I change only the child’s measurement age. The slope rises from 0.14 at 25 to 0.31 at 40. Early incomes hide differences that emerge later. The small dips along the way, such as at ages 31 and 36, are sampling noise in this one simulated sample, not part of the pattern.








Figure 2: Changing the child’s measurement age changes the estimated persistence even with the same parents and families.





This illustrates life-cycle bias. Children with higher lasting incomes have steeper early income growth in the model. If everyone’s income grew by the same percentage, that alone would not change the slope. The age pattern is deliberately built in, not discovered in real data. Haider and Solon explain why current earnings can represent lifetime earnings differently at different ages.
Even averaging the child’s ages 25 through 29 gives only 0.17. More observations still describe an early career. Real data also require survey weights and decisions about missing years and zero incomes, which this complete, positive-income, equally weighted simulation avoids.
The main takeaways are:

Join on the full person ID, and remove duplicate family-years from two-parent links before counting or averaging.
Average several years to reduce temporary fluctuations that can make mobility look stronger.
Compare suitable ages too. Averaging early earnings does not make them representative of a whole career.
